item.title: Missing incomes can make inequality look smaller than it is
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
Income is one of the questions that people most often refuse to answer in surveys. If the people who do not answer were just a random subset of the sample (MCAR), deleting them would only cost precision. But non-response is rarely random: very rich and, sometimes, very poor households answer less often.

When high incomes are more often missing, the respondents look more equal than the population, and the Gini index computed with the complete cases underestimates inequality. Two popular fixes make things worse:

  • Mean imputation gives every non-respondent the same income, so it removes inequality by construction.
  • Regression imputation without a random residual places every imputed value on the regression line, with the same effect.

If non-response depends on variables that we observe for everybody, such as education, age or region (MAR), multiple imputation with these variables in the imputation model removes most of the bias and gives honest margins of error. If it depends on income itself (MNAR), no standard method is enough, and sensitivity analyses are needed.

You can see all this with your own eyes in the missing data simulator: choose a distribution, a percentage of missing data and a mechanism, and compare six methods. This is the topic of objective OG2 of GiniUs.

item.title: In one minute: Exploring and correcting the bias in the estimation of the Gini measure of inequality
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
J.F. Muñoz, P.J. Moya-Fernández and E. Álvarez-Verdejo (Sociological Methods & Research, 2025; JCR Q1). Read the article.

The question. There are many formulas to estimate the Gini index from a sample. Do they all give the right answer?

What they found.

  • One popular formula strongly overestimates inequality when inequality is low.
  • With skewed and unequal data, the usual estimators tend to underestimate inequality.
  • Bootstrap and jackknife corrections reduce the bias, and a simple criterion tells when to use them.

Why it matters. Differences in inequality between countries, regions or groups can come from the formula used, not from real differences. Choosing the right estimator avoids wrong conclusions.

All the videos are on the page Our research in one minute.

item.title: In one minute: A practical guide to proper estimation and inference of the Gini index by avoiding often encountered methodological pitfalls
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
J.F. Muñoz, J.M. Pavía and E. Álvarez-Verdejo (Social Indicators Research, 2026; JCR Q1). Read the article.

The question. The Gini index is the most used measure of inequality. But computing it from data is error-prone. Do common practices give wrong numbers and wrong margins of error?

What they found.

  • Some widely used formulas give inaccurate estimates of inequality.
  • A popular regression-based method seriously underestimates the margin of error when incomes are very skewed and unequal.
  • Jackknife methods give the most accurate margins of error.

Why it matters. Margins of error that are too small can make us believe inequality changed when it did not. The paper gives practical recommendations and the free R package giniVarCI.

All the videos are on the page Our research in one minute.

item.title: In one minute: The “Happy and Poor” paradox: why do some poor people report being very happy?
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
J. Guardiola, F. García-Quero and A. García-García (Applied Research in Quality of Life, 2026; JCR Q1). Read the article.

The question. Many people living in poverty say they are very happy. How can that be?

Six explanations.

  • Their basic needs are met and they are satisfied in key areas of life; they adapt to hardship and have modest aspirations.
  • Scientists and policymakers may misjudge how well they are doing.
  • Their culture supports happiness, and maldevelopment has not eroded it.

Why it matters. Poverty is not only a lack of income. Listening to how people evaluate their own lives helps design better development policies.

item.title: In one minute: Innovation and poverty-related income gaps in Europe: evidence from the North–South divide
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
P.A. Cano-Chica, V.E. Yáñez-Justicia, A. Rodríguez-Copete, E. Álvarez-Verdejo and A.J. López-Montoya (Journal of Poverty, 2026; JCR Q3). Read the article.

The question. How are innovation and entrepreneurship related to the income gaps that affect the poorest households in Europe?

What the study analyses.

  • How innovation dynamics interact with income inequality and poverty-related vulnerability.
  • Differences between Northern and Southern Europe.
  • Changes within countries over time and differences between countries.

Why it matters. Innovation policies can widen or narrow income gaps. Knowing where and how helps to design fairer innovation policies in Europe.

All the videos are on the page Our research in one minute.

item.title: In one minute: Inequalities in talents’ earnings: a tale of two European countries
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
T. Addabbo and C. Mussida (Social Indicators Research, 2025; JCR Q1). Read the article.

The question. Are young graduates paid differently in Italy and in Germany? And are women paid less than men?

What they found.

  • The wage gap against Italian talents grew in 2022, mainly because the same qualifications are paid less.
  • The gap grew more for women, especially at the top.
  • Gender gap among talents: Italy from 10% to 22.5%; Germany from 27.5% to 15%.

Why it matters. Better pay and conditions in Germany help explain why young Italian talents move there. Policies are needed to attract and keep talent.

item.title: In one minute: Dynamic spatio-temporal modelling of tourism impact on income inequality and polarization: inbound and domestic flows in the EU
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
C.M. Llorca-Rodríguez, A.C. Casas-Jurado, R.M. García-Fernández and J. Chica-Olmo (Papers in Regional Science, 2025; JCR Q2, ABS 3). Read the article.

The question. Does tourism make income more equal in European regions, or less?

What they found.

  • Overall, tourism and inequality follow an inverted-U shape.
  • Inbound tourism increases inequality and polarization in destinations; domestic tourism reduces them.
  • Both types improve the income distribution of neighbouring regions.

Why it matters. Useful for the EU Cohesion Policy: domestic tourism supports cohesion, and social protection (education, health, unemployment and retirement) should be strengthened.

All the videos are on the page Our research in one minute.

item.title: In one minute: Does tourism reduce socio-economic inequality? Insights from the pandemic based on space and time models for the EU
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
C.M. Llorca-Rodríguez, R.M. García-Fernández and J. Chica-Olmo (Economia Politica, 2026; JCR Q2). Read the article.

The question. Does tourism help to reduce poverty and social exclusion in European regions?

What they found.

  • International (inbound) tourism increases poverty and social exclusion in destination regions.
  • Domestic tourism reduces them, in destinations and in neighbouring regions.
  • Some other effects are statistically significant but economically very small.

Why it matters. Tourism does not reduce poverty by itself. Market structures, labour regulation, competitiveness and social protection decide who benefits.

All the videos are on the page Our research in one minute.

item.title: In one minute: Does economic growth drive equitable water and sanitation access? Assessing inequality reduction across 64 nations
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
M. García-López, S. López-Ruiz and G. Cuadrado-Quesada (Sustainable Development, 2026; JCR Q1). Read the article.

The question. When a country grows richer, does access to water and sanitation become more equal?

What they found.

  • Growth improves access overall, but the poorest and rural populations are left behind.
  • Inequality in sanitation is not related to growth.
  • Unequal access to water also holds back GDP per capita.

Why it matters. Growth alone will not deliver water and sanitation for all (SDG 6). Effective governance and efficient water use are needed.

All the videos are on the page Our research in one minute.

item.title: Welcome to the new GiniUs website
item.dc:creator: GiniUs team
item.description:
GiniUs studies how to measure inequality reliably with the Gini index: which estimator to use, how large its bias can be, how to obtain margins of error that can be trusted, and how to deal with missing incomes. The project, funded by the Spanish State Research Agency (PID2022-136235NB-I00), is now in its fourth and last year.

The new website brings together the results of the project and several tools that run in your browser, without installing anything:

  • a Gini index calculator for your own data, with jackknife and bootstrap confidence intervals and the Lorenz curve;
  • an interactive bias explorer that reproduces the Monte Carlo studies of the project;
  • a missing data simulator that compares complete-case analysis, single imputation and multiple imputation under the MCAR, MAR and MNAR mechanisms;
  • R exercises, including the R package giniVarCI running in the browser;
  • an inequality observatory with official Gini indices from Eurostat, the World Bank and INE.

In this blog we will publish short posts on new articles, software releases, seminars and practical advice on measuring inequality. You can follow it through the RSS feed or by subscribing.
